question: J009 — RLS to rust-analyzer: when sharing the compiler was not enough

sources.name: RFC 1317 — Rust Language Server
sources.note: Original design goals: compiler-as-library, long-running service, database/work queue, planned lazy compilation and compiler reuse; explicitly identifies invalidation/cancellation refactoring as a hard requirement for keeping rustc alive.

sources.name: RLS architecture at archived repository tip
sources.note: Documents implemented save-analysis pipeline, in-process rustc invocations for dirty crates, dependency JSON cache, Cargo orchestration, VFS overlays, build squashing, and Racer coordination.

sources.name: 2019-11-18 IDE team meeting — Why 2 IDEs?
sources.note: Contemporary Rust project account contrasts rust-analyzer's lazy performance/flexible API with RLS precision from rustc and describes save-analysis as a static compiler-derived view.

sources.name: rust-analyzer first release
sources.note: Explains persistent on-demand architecture, per-keystroke RLS whole-body rechecking, reuse of name-resolution results, 2020 rust-analyzer limitations, and cargo-check-on-save as a separate precision path.

sources.name: RFC 2912 — Transition to rust-analyzer as official LSP
sources.note: Records the architectural trade: save-analysis precision versus on-demand latency, accepted short-term duplicate compiler logic, explicit divergence risk, library-ification goal, and the alternative of porting the approach back into rustc.

sources.name: RLS deprecation announcement
sources.note: Rust Dev Tools Team states RLS architecture had limitations for low-latency, high-quality interactive responses and announces migration to rust-analyzer.

sources.name: Current rust-analyzer architecture
sources.note: Current design: explicit in-memory inputs, lazy derived state, error-tolerant syntax, incremental HIR, transactional AnalysisHost plus immutable Analysis snapshots, partial operation during broken builds, separate flycheck/toolchain integration, isolated proc-macro process.

sources.name: Early rust-analyzer architecture notes
sources.note: Shows error-tolerant parser/syntax-tree work at the start of rust-analyzer development. A later 2018 architecture update already described stateful analysis handing out immutable snapshots and on-demand query machinery.

sources.name: Anneal principles and design contract
sources.note: Used only to bound applicability: useful partial information must remain distinguishable from successful verification, and formal claims come from an accepted checking boundary.

limits: No RLS, rust-analyzer, rustc, Lean, or Anneal executable was run for this report.

The report does not estimate current rust-analyzer/rustc semantic divergence frequency; historical sources establish that divergence existed and the current architecture remains a distinct analysis engine.
The 2020 library-ification vision is treated as intent, not as proof that rustc and rust-analyzer later converged to one semantic implementation.
Anneal conclusions are derived conditional analysis, not adopted design policy.
